In [[birational geometry]], the '''Cremona group''', named after [[Luigi Cremona]], is [[Birational geometry#Birational automorphism groups|the group of birational automorphisms]] of the <math>n</math>-dimensional [[projective space]] over a [[Field (mathematics)|field]] {{nowrap|<math>k</math>}}, also known as '''Cremona transformations'''. It is denoted by <math>Cr(\mathbb{P}^n(k))</math>, <math>Bir(\mathbb{P}^n(k))</math> or <math>Cr_n(k)</math>.

== Historical origins ==
The Cremona group was introduced by the Italian mathematician {{harvs|txt|authorlink=Luigi Cremona|last=Cremona|year1=1863|year2=1865|first=Luigi}}.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Trkovská |first=D. |date=2008 |title=Luigi Cremona and his Transformations |url=https://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/document?repid=rep1&type=pdf&doi=1768e9cb4c25bf14b88689590b872b53a0874369 |journal=WDS'08 Proceedings of Contributed Papers |publisher=MatfyzPress |pages=32–37}}</ref> In retrospect, the British mathematician [[Isaac Newton]] is considered a founder of "the theory of Cremona transformations", having developed his "''organic construction''" to perform birational maps of the projective plane and applied them to [[resolution of singularities|resolve]] curve singularities, nearly two centuries before Cremona.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Shkolenok |first=Galina A. |date=1972 |title=Geometrical Constructions Equivalent to Non-Linear Algebraic Transformations of the Plane in Newton's Early Papers |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/41133348 |journal=Archive for History of Exact Sciences |volume=9 |issue=1 |pages=22–44 |doi=10.1007/BF00348538 |jstor=41133348 |issn=0003-9519}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bloye |first1=Nicole |last2=Huggett |first2=Stephen |year=2011 |title=Newton, the geometer |url=https://stephenhuggett.com/Newton.pdf |url-status=dead |journal=Newsletter of the European Mathematical Society |issue=82 |pages=19–27 |mr=2896438 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230308041757/http://stephenhuggett.com/Newton.pdf |archive-date=8 March 2023 |access-date=19 February 2023}}</ref> The mathematician [[Hilda Phoebe Hudson]] made contributions in the 1900s as well.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Hilda Hudson - Biography |url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Hudson/ |access-date=2025-04-19 |website=Maths History |language=en}}</ref>

== Basic properties ==
The Cremona group is naturally identified with the [[automorphism group]] <math>\mathrm{Aut}_k(k(x_1, ..., x_n)) </math> of the [[rational function|field of the rational function]]s in <math>n</math> [[Indeterminate (variable)|indeterminates]] over <math>k</math>. Here, the field <math>k(x_1, ..., x_n) </math> is a pure [[transcendental extension]] of <math>k</math>, with [[transcendence degree]] <math>n</math>.

The [[projective general linear group]] <math>\mathrm{PGL}_{n+1}</math> is contained in <math>Cr_n</math>. The two are equal only when <math>n=0</math> or <math>n=1</math>, in which case both the numerator and the denominator of a transformation must be linear.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Cremona group - Encyclopedia of Mathematics |url=https://encyclopediaofmath.org/index.php?title=Cremona_group |access-date=2025-05-30 |website=encyclopediaofmath.org}}</ref>

A longlasting question from [[Federigo Enriques]] concerns the [[Simple group|simplicity]] of the Cremona group. It has been now mostly answered.<ref name=":0" />

==The Cremona group in 2 dimensions==

In two dimensions, [[Max Noether]] and [[Guido Castelnuovo]] showed that the complex Cremona group is generated by the standard quadratic transformation <math>[x:y:z]\mapsto [yz:zx:xy]</math>, along with <math>\mathrm{PGL}(3,k)</math>, though there was some controversy about whether their proofs were correct. {{harvtxt|Gizatullin|1983}} gave a complete [[Generators and relations|set of relations for these generators]]. The structure of this group is still not well understood, though there has been a lot of work on finding elements or subgroups of it. 
*{{harvtxt|Cantat|Lamy|2010}} showed that for an [[Algebraic closure|algebraically closed]] field <math>k</math>, the group <math>Cr_2(k)</math> is not [[Simple group|simple]].
*{{harvtxt|Blanc|2010}} showed that it is topologically simple for the [[Zariski topology]].{{
efn|name=fn1|1=I.e. it does not contain any non-trivial [[Closed subgroup|closed]] normal strict subgroup.}}
*For the finite subgroups of the Cremona group see {{harvtxt|Dolgachev|Iskovskikh|2009}}.
*{{harvtxt|Zimmermann|2018}} computed the [[abelianization]] of <math>Cr_2(\mathbb{R})</math>. From this, she deduces that there is no analogue of Noether–Castelnuovo theorem in this context.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |date=2020-11-30 |title=A propos des travaux de Susanna Zimmermann, médaille de bronze du CNRS 2020 {{!}} CNRS Mathématiques |url=https://www.insmi.cnrs.fr/fr/cnrsinfo/propos-des-travaux-de-susanna-zimmermann-medaille-de-bronze-du-cnrs-2020 |access-date=2025-05-30 |website=www.insmi.cnrs.fr |language=fr}}</ref>

== Geiser and Bertini involutions ==

The '''Geiser involution''' and '''Bertini involution''' are two of the classical non-linear involutions of the plane Cremona group.<ref name="BB2000">{{cite journal |last1=Bayle |first1=Lionel |last2=Beauville |first2=Arnaud |author-link2=Arnaud Beauville |title=Birational involutions of P2 |journal=Asian Journal of Mathematics |volume=4 |issue=1 |year=2000 |pages=11–18}}</ref><ref name="Dolgachev 2009">{{harvtxt|Dolgachev|Iskovskikh|2009}}</ref> They arise from [[Del Pezzo surface]]s of degree 2 and degree 1, respectively.

A Geiser involution is obtained by blowing up seven points of <math>\mathbb{P}^2</math> in [[general position]], producing a Del Pezzo surface <math>S</math> of degree 2. The anticanonical linear system <math>|-K_S|</math> defines a double cover <math>S\to \mathbb{P}^2</math> branched over a smooth plane quartic, and the deck transformation is the Geiser involution.<ref name="Dolgachev 2012">{{harvtxt|Dolgachev|2012}}</ref><ref name="Dolgachev 2009"/> Via the blow-down <math>S\to \mathbb{P}^2</math>, this becomes a birational involution of the plane. Classically, if <math>p_1,\dots,p_7</math> are the seven base points, then a general point <math>x</math> is sent to the ninth base point of the pencil of cubic curves through <math>p_1,\dots,p_7,x</math>.<ref name="BB2000" /><ref name="Dolgachev 2009"/> The resulting Cremona transformation has degree 8.<ref name="Dolgachev 2009"/>

Similarly, blowing up eight points of <math>\mathbb{P}^2</math> in general position produces a Del Pezzo surface of degree 1. The linear system <math>|-2K_S|</math> defines a double cover of a [[quadric cone]] in <math>\mathbb{P}^3</math>, and its deck transformation is the Bertini involution.<ref name="Dolgachev 2012"/><ref name="Dolgachev 2009"/> In classical plane terms, if <math>p_1,\dots,p_8</math> are the base points, then for a general point <math>x</math> one considers the net of sextics through <math>p_1,\dots,p_8,x</math> that are singular at <math>p_1,\dots,p_8</math>; the Bertini involution sends <math>x</math> to the fixed point of this net.<ref name="BB2000" /> Its degree is 17.<ref name="Dolgachev 2009"/>

Over an algebraically closed field of characteristic different from 2, Bayle and Beauville's modern proof of the classical theorem on birational involutions of the plane shows that every non-trivial involution in <math>\mathrm{Bir}(\mathbb{P}^2)</math> is conjugate to exactly one of three types: a de Jonquières involution, a Geiser involution, or a Bertini involution.<ref name="BB2000" /> The normalized fixed curve of a Geiser involution is a non-hyperelliptic curve of genus 3, while that of a Bertini involution is a non-hyperelliptic curve of genus 4 whose canonical model lies on a singular quadric.<ref name="BB2000" /> Consequently, conjugacy classes of Geiser involutions are parametrized by isomorphism classes of non-hyperelliptic genus-3 curves, and conjugacy classes of Bertini involutions by isomorphism classes of non-hyperelliptic genus-4 curves whose canonical model lies on a singular quadric.<ref name="BB2000" />

==The Cremona group in higher dimensions==

There is little known about the structure of the Cremona group in three dimensions and higher though many elements of it have been described.

There is no easy analogue of the Noether–Castelnouvo theorem, as {{harvtxt|Hudson|1927}} showed that the Cremona group in dimension at least 3 is not generated by its elements of degree bounded by any fixed integer.

{{harvtxt|Blanc|2010}} showed that it is (linearly) [[Connected space|connected]], answering a question of {{harvtxt|Serre|2010}}. Later, {{harvtxt|Blanc|Zimmermann|2018}} showed that for any infinite field <math>k</math>, the group <math>Cr_n(k)</math> is topologically simple{{efn|name=fn1}} for the [[Zariski topology]], and even for the [[euclidean topology]] when <math>k</math> is a [[local field]].

{{harvtxt|Blanc|Lamy|Zimmermann|2021}} proved that when <math>k</math> is a [[Subfield (mathematics)|subfield]] of the [[complex number]]s and <math>n\geq 3</math>, then <math>Cr_n(k)</math> is not a [[simple group]].

==De Jonquières groups==

A De Jonquières group is a subgroup of a Cremona group of the following form.<ref>{{cite arXiv |eprint=1110.2410 |last1=Popov |first1=Vladimir L. |title=Some subgroups of the Cremona groups |date=2011 |class=math.AG }}</ref> Pick a [[transcendence basis]] <math>x_1, ..., x_n</math> for a [[field extension]] of <math>k</math>. Then a De Jonquières group is the subgroup of automorphisms of <math>k(x_1, ...,x_n)</math> mapping the subfield <math>k(x_1, ...,x_r)</math> into itself for some <math>r\leq n</math>. It has a [[normal subgroup]] given by the Cremona group of automorphisms of <math>k(x_1, ..., x_n)</math> over the field <math>k(x_1, ..., x_r)</math>, and the [[quotient group]] is the Cremona group of <math>k(x_1, ..., x_r)</math> over the field <math>k</math>. It can also be regarded as the group of birational automorphisms of the [[fiber bundle]] <math>\mathbb{P}^r\times \mathbb{P}^{n-r} \to \mathbb{P}^r</math>.

When <math> n=2</math> and <math> r=1</math> the De Jonquières group is the group of Cremona transformations fixing a [[pencil of lines]] through a given point, and is the [[semidirect product]] of <math>\mathrm{PGL}_2(k)</math> and <math>\mathrm{PGL}_2(k(t))</math>.
